title: The Letter of Greywater Bay
premise: When insurance investigator Jonah Quintana is handed the recovered diary of Marina Voss—a woman who vanished from Greywater Bay seven years ago—she notices the entries continue for three weeks past the official date of disappearance. Following the diary's coded references, Jonah uncovers a network of townspeople who helped Marina fake her death to escape her powerful husband, Aldous Voss, whose shipping fortune was about to pass to her under a new will. As Jonah closes in on the living witness everyone believes dead, she discovers her own photographic memory holds the key: she once catalogued a document proving Aldous forged Marina's death certificate, and he will kill to keep it buried. In the end, Jonah chooses testimony over invisibility, exposing Aldous at the inheritance hearing and reuniting Marina with the found family that hid her—while claiming a place in it herself.
about_author: Wren Sandoval is a former coastal claims adjuster who spent a decade reading other people's losses before writing her own. She lives in a fog-bound harbor town where she keeps meticulous files and answers letters no one else will.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Small Towns
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Establishes Greywater Bay, Jonah's photographic memory, and her careful invisibility among neighbors whose secrets she has memorized but never spoken. A cold-case box arrives at her office: Marina Voss's diary, dredged from the bay. Emotional beat: the comfort of order beginning to crack.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Reading the diary at night, Jonah finds dated entries continuing twenty-two days beyond Marina's disappearance, including one that names 'the grey house' and warns 'he counts the boats.' Emotional beat: dread disguised as curiosity; the case stops being paperwork.

chapters.title: The Widow's Husband
chapters.summary: Jonah interviews Aldous Voss at the Voss Shipping offices, cataloguing his rehearsed grief against seven-year-old claim photos where his cufflinks differ. He mentions her by name unprompted. Emotional beat: first direct contact with danger, masked as courtesy.

chapters.title: Grey House, Grey Water
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. She locates the grey house—an abandoned pilot's cottage—and finds fresh boot prints and a hidden cache: Marina's real wedding ring and a bus ticket never used. Emotional beat: proof of life, and the vertigo of knowing something the whole town denies.

chapters.title: Everyone Swears She's Dead
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs via Jonah's interviews. The diner owner, the harbormaster, and the pastor each give alibis too identical to be honest. Jonah realizes they aren't lying about a murder—they're protecting someone. Emotional beat: the town as a wall of kind, coordinated silence.

chapters.title: What I Filed Under F
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Searching her own memory archive, Jonah recalls processing a death certificate seven years ago signed by a doctor who died before he could have examined the body. Emotional beat: horror that her perfect memory makes her a witness—and a target.

chapters.title: The Doctor Who Signed Too Soon
chapters.summary: Jonah visits the late Dr. Pell's widow, who slips her an unsent letter addressed to Marina. The letter reveals Pell helped stage the death and feared Aldous had discovered it. Emotional beat: grief for a good man complicit in a necessary lie.

chapters.title: Aldous Counts the Boats
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, tense and clipped. Her office is searched; her case file on the Voss estate is gone. She notices a boat following her along the shore road. Emotional beat: the hunter realizing she has become the hunted.

chapters.title: The Found Family
chapters.summary: POV shift to Ruth Okafor, retired ferry cook, who has been leaving food at the grey house for seven years. Ruth confronts Jonah, testing whether she can be trusted. Emotional beat: fierce tenderness; the first offer of belonging Jonah has ever received.

chapters.title: Twenty-Two Days
chapters.summary: Jonah reconstructs Marina's post-disappearance timeline from the diary: Marina stayed in the grey house waiting for a boat that never came because Aldous bought the ferry captain's silence. Emotional beat: sympathy deepening into resolve—Marina wasn't fleeing alone; she was abandoned mid-escape.

chapters.title: Inheritance in Escrow
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The Voss trust is set to dissolve on its seventh anniversary; if Marina is declared legally dead next week, everything passes to Aldous permanently. The clock becomes explicit. Emotional beat: urgency sharpening every choice.

chapters.title: The Ferry Captain's Confession
chapters.summary: POV of Captain Ives, drunk and terrified, who admits to Jonah that Aldous paid him to skip the pickup and swear Marina drowned. He gives her a key to a marina locker. Emotional beat: guilt finally breaking the town's seal of silence.

chapters.title: Locker 114
chapters.summary: Jonah opens the locker: inside are the original death certificate with Pell's hesitant signature, Aldous's forged addendum, and photographs of Marina alive, taken last spring. Someone has been checking on her. Emotional beat: hope arriving wrapped in evidence.

chapters.title: Photographic
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, introspective. Flashbacks show how her memory isolated her as a child—reciting what adults wanted forgotten. She understands Marina's disappearance and her own invisibility are the same survival strategy. Emotional beat: identity theme crystallizing; loneliness named.

chapters.title: They Know You Have It
chapters.summary: Ruth warns Jonah that Aldous's man was seen asking about her at the diner. That night Jonah's apartment is ransacked; the diary is stolen, but not the copies she mailed to herself. Emotional beat: fear met with the investigator's stubborn craft.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Jonah attends the presumptive-death hearing as a spectator, watching Aldous perform bereavement while the judge prepares to sign. She says nothing—but memorizes every face in the room, including a veiled woman in the back row. Emotional beat: restraint stretched to breaking.

chapters.title: The Veiled Woman
chapters.summary: Jonah follows the woman from the courthouse to the grey house and comes face to face with Marina Voss—alive, weathered, furious that Jonah has endangered the people who saved her. Emotional beat: the mystery's heart exposed; two women who erased themselves recognizing each other.

chapters.title: What Marina Chose
chapters.summary: Marina's POV. She recounts the marriage, the control, the staged drowning, and why she stayed hidden even after Aldous stopped searching: leaving would destroy Ruth, Ives, and Pell's memory. Emotional beat: the cost of survival; found family as both shelter and cage.

chapters.title: Aldous at the Door
chapters.summary: Climax begins. Aldous, tipped off by the stolen diary's trail, arrives at the grey house with his fixer. Jonah triggers the harbormaster's old foghorn signal—the town's secret alarm—and Ruth, Ives, and half the fishing fleet converge. Emotional beat: terror answered by solidarity.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Climax. Cornered on the dock, Aldous offers Jonah money for the documents; she recites, verbatim, his forged certificate line by line before the assembled town and the sheriff he thought he owned. Marina steps out of the fog, unveiled. Emotional beat: memory weaponized into truth; invisibility voluntarily ended.

chapters.title: Probate and Fog
chapters.summary: Falling action. Aldous is arrested; the trust hearing reconvenes and recognizes Marina alive, who redirects the inheritance into a fund for the town's lost and missing. Ives turns himself in; Pell's letter is finally delivered. Emotional beat: justice without triumphalism; debts acknowledged.

chapters.title: Filed Under Q
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, epilogue. Months later, Jonah keeps her office but no longer keeps her distance—Sunday dinners at Ruth's, Marina teaching her to read tides. She opens a new case folder labeled with her own name and writes the first entry. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; the invisible woman choosing to be seen.
